packets.target_claim: The new picking-assistance scanner explains most (more than half) of Site A's lower order-completion time relative to Site B.

evidence.E1: Across the first 8 weeks after rollout, Site A's mean order-completion time was 18% lower than Site B's.
evidence.E2: After adjustment for order size, product mix, and shift, Site A's estimated advantage was 7%.
evidence.E3: The scanner rollout at Site A began in the same week as the largest observed improvement in completion time.
evidence.E4: During the 6 weeks before rollout, Site A was already about 5% faster than Site B.
evidence.E5: During four shifts when Site A's scanner was unavailable, Site A remained about 6% faster than Site B.
evidence.E6: Mean worker tenure was 2.8 years at Site A and 1.4 years at Site B.
evidence.E7: A small randomized crossover involving 40 workers estimated that scanner use reduced individual picking time by 4%, with a 95% confidence interval from -1% to 9%.
evidence.E8: A timestamp audit found that Site A's workflow system closes tasks about 1.5 minutes earlier than Site B's system because of a configuration difference, enough to explain roughly 2 percentage points of the raw gap.

packets.target_claim: Printer X's higher nozzle-temperature setting explains most (more than half) of its higher tensile strength relative to Printer Y.

evidence.E1: Across 8 production batches, coupons from Printer X had 14% higher mean tensile strength than coupons from Printer Y.
evidence.E2: After adjustment for filament lot, humidity, build orientation, and layer height, the estimated Printer X advantage was 6%.
evidence.E3: Printer X's nozzle-temperature setting changed in the same batch series in which the largest strength improvement appeared.
evidence.E4: Across six historical batches before the temperature-setting change, Printer X was already about 4% stronger than Printer Y.
evidence.E5: In four production runs where Printer X used Printer Y's nozzle-temperature setting, Printer X still produced coupons about 5% stronger.
evidence.E6: Printer X's filament was dried for about 6 hours before printing, compared with about 3 hours for Printer Y.
evidence.E7: A randomized paired build of 40 coupon pairs in which only nozzle temperature was changed estimated a 3% strength increase, with a 95% confidence interval from -2% to 8%.
evidence.E8: A load-frame calibration audit found that the test setup used for Printer X reads about 1.5% higher force near the relevant test range.
